analysis.one_liner: Taxes Wall Street trades at fractions of a percent to fund social and infrastructure programs.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 39 House sponsors and cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a small tax on each trade of stocks, bonds, and derivatives: 0.5% on stock trades, 0.1% on bond trades, and a tiny fraction of a percent on other financial contracts. Exchanges and brokers would collect the tax at the time of each trade. Low- and moderate-income households would get a refundable-style credit reimbursing any of the tax they paid, up to income limits of $50,000 for singles and $75,000 for joint filers. The sponsors intended the revenue for child care, infrastructure, health programs, and global health and climate programs, and argued the tax would also curb high-frequency trading that they said creates market volatility.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income families, through a credit that refunds any tax they pay on their own trades, plus the programs the revenue would fund: child care, Social Security, infrastructure, Medicare and Medicaid expansion, education and job training, housing assistance, and international health and climate programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and moderate-income households and public programs

how_it_helps.text: Households with modified adjusted gross income under $50,000 ($75,000 for joint filers) would get a tax credit equal to the full financial transaction tax they paid, so ordinary savers would not bear the tax.

The bill's findings state the tax could generate hundreds of billions of dollars annually, which the sponsors directed toward the social safety net, child care, infrastructure, clean energy, education, housing assistance, and global health programs.

The tax applies to every transfer of ownership in stocks, most bonds, and derivatives, catching the high-frequency trading the bill says makes up as much as 70% of market volume and contributes to price volatility.

analysis.who_pays: High-volume traders, hedge funds, and other large financial institutions, which would pay the tax on each trade; exchanges and brokers would be responsible for collecting and remitting it. The cost of high-frequency trading strategies would rise the most.

drawbacks.text: Taxes on trades are ultimately built into the cost of trading, so some cost would likely reach ordinary investors through fund expenses and trading spreads, even though the bill's findings assert the impact on the average investor is negligible.

A tax on US trades creates an incentive to route trading through foreign venues; the bill tries to counter this by taxing any purchase where the buyer or seller is a US person, but enforcement against avoidance would depend on regulations the Treasury Secretary would have to write, and the bill gives the Commissioner unilateral authority to rescind penalties with no judicial appeal.

Revenue estimates for financial transaction taxes are highly uncertain because trading volume can fall sharply in response; the bill itself cites only that economists project the tax 'could' generate hundreds of billions annually, not a firm figure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is small per trade (0.5% on stocks, 0.1% on bonds, 0.005% on derivatives) and low-income households are fully reimbursed through the credit, so the direct burden on ordinary savers would be limited while the revenue potential is large. The genuine risks are that trading migrates to unregulated venues, revenue falls short of projections, and enforcement relies on bureaucratic discretion with limited oversight. On balance this is a significant redistribution proposal whose costs fall mainly on high-volume finance and whose benefits would be broad, but its revenue estimates deserve skepticism.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never held a hearing or advanced it, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Keith Ellison introduced the Inclusive Prosperity Act of 2017 on February 16, 2017, with 17 original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
A total of 38 members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats, and no further action was ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-frequency trading firms, brokerages, and other large financial institutions avoided a new tax on every trade, and their customers avoided any pass-through costs, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that would have paid the tax

industries.industry: Securities trading firms, hedge funds, and high-frequency traders
industries.note: The bill would tax every purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives, with the 0.5% stock rate falling hardest on high-volume strategies; the bill's sponsors argue this also curbs volatility-driven speculation. Ordinary savers would be reimbursed through the credit, so the industry's cost would not be fully passed to them.

Exchanges and brokers would be legally responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on each covered trade, adding compliance and operational costs, though the tax itself would fall on the trading activity. Short-term debt with maturities of 60 days or less and certain securities-lending transactions are exempted.

The bill directs revenue toward child care, Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid expansion, education, housing assistance, transportation, water infrastructure, and clean energy, along with international health and climate programs.
